#7629. Justices Thomas and Alito on State Requirements That Continuing Professional Education Discuss Certain Topics

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v. Yip, joined by Justice Alito (Justice Gorsuch voted to grant the petition, but didn't sign on to the dissent):

In 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes. The Ninth Circuit held that First Amendment scrutiny did not apply to this compelled-speech requirement because the breadth of California's CME regulation renders the content of any CME course government speech, not private speech. That logic fundamentally misunderstands this Court's precedents and the Constitution. First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.

I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine. At a minimum, the Ninth Circuit misapplied Shurtleff v. Boston (2022), which instructs courts to identify government speech by considering (1) "the history of the expression at issue," (2) "the public's likely perception as to who (the government or a private person) is speaking," and (3) "the extent to which the government has actively shaped or controlled the expression." The Ninth Circuit collapsed those distinct inquiries, focusing on the breadth of the government's regulatory scheme at each step. More fundamentally, however, Shurtleff is leading courts astray.

I joined Justice ALITO's concurrence in Shurtleff, which warned that the majority's three-factor test could cause courts to conclude that extensive government regulation transforms a private message into government speech exempt from First Amendment scrutiny. As the Ninth Circuit's decision shows, those concerns were prescient. This Court should reconsider whether the Shurtleff test is the proper mode of analysis for identifying government speech…

California-licensed physicians are required to complete 50 hours of approved CME every two years. Credit-eligible CME courses are often organized by private entities, certified by private accreditors, and taught by private instructors. The State does not preapprove course content but reserves the right to audit courses for compliance with its CME standards.

The Medical Board of California "adopt[s] and administer[s] [CME] standards," few of which relate to course content. In addition, the State requires that CME courses broadly relate to the medical profession. They must "serve to maintain, develop, or increase the knowledge, skills, and professional performance that a physician and surgeon uses to provide care, or to improve the quality of care provided to patients." In 2019, however, the California Legislature added a requirement that after January 1, 2022, all CME courses must "contain curriculum that includes the understanding of implicit bias." To satisfy that requirement, CME courses must contain "[e]xamples of how implicit bias affects perceptions and treatment decisions of physicians and surgeons, leading to disparities in health outcomes" or "[s]trategies to address how unintended biases in decisionmaking may contribute to health care disparities."

Petitioners Dr. Azadeh Khatibi and Do No Harm do not want to speak California's preferred message on implicit bias, and they challenged § 2190.1(d) as compelling speech in violation of the First Amendment. Dr. Khatibi, a California-licensed ophthalmologist, creates and teaches CME courses. She "disagrees that implicit bias is the primary factor driving disparities in healthcare" and does not want to devote time to the subject during her courses. Do No Harm is a nonprofit corporation. At least one of its members teaches CME courses and believes that implicit bias trainings "have not been shown to successfully reduce barriers to healthcare, and instead risk infecting healthcare decisions with divisive and discriminatory ideas." Yet, California's implicit-bias-training requirement leaves petitioners no choice but to discuss the topic in a way that affirms the State's view that implicit bias causes "disparities in health outcomes…..

The Ninth Circuit held that all three Shurtleff factors indicate that "CMEs eligible for Board credit constitute government speech." At every step of the analysis, the Ninth Circuit emphasized the breadth of the State's regulation. Considering history, the court noted that California "has long regulated the practice of medicine as an exercise of the police power" and has "adopted, updated, and enforced CME standards." Considering the public's likely perception of the speaker in a CME course, the court reasoned that "licensees could attribute approved CMEs' content to California" because "their profession is heavily regulated." Considering the extent to which the government has shaped the expression, the court cited "California's extraordinary control over accredited CMEs." As Judge VanDyke explained in his dissent from the denial of rehearing en banc, the panel's "approach boil[ed] down to a single-factor analysis: does the government 'heavily' or 'actively' regulate CMEs?" …

In its blinkered application of the Shurtleff factors, the Ninth Circuit lost sight of the core government-speech inquiry: whether the government is "speak[ing] for itself or … regulat[ing] private expression."

The government-speech doctrine occupies a narrow corner of our First Amendment jurisprudence. The First Amendment protects the people's right of free speech against government interference; it does not prevent the government from speaking for itself. "But courts must be very careful when a government claims that speech by one or more private speakers is actually government speech." "If private speech could be passed off as government speech by simply affixing a government seal of approval, government could … muffle the expression of disfavored viewpoints," or, as here, require private speakers to convey government messages without facing any constitutional scrutiny.

This Court has thus exercised "great caution" before characterizing a message as government speech. In Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Assn (2005), we held that government-sponsored beef ads constituted government speech because the government determined "the overarching message" of the ads, helped develop proposals for the ads, reviewed every ad "for substance and for wording," and the Secretary of Agriculture "exercise[d] final approval authority over every word used in every" ad. In Pleasant Grove City v. Summum (2009), we held that the permanent display of monuments in a public park was government speech because the City "effectively controlled the messages sent by the monuments in the Park by exercising final approval authority over their selection." And, in Walker v. Texas Div., Sons of Confederate Veterans, Inc. (2015), we held that the messages on government-issued license plates, over which the State "maintain[ed] direct control," were government speech.

Since Walker—which we have described as the "outer boun[d] of the government-speech doctrine," Matal v. Tam (2017)—we have been careful to distinguish between government control over messages and government control over the broader scheme through which the messages are communicated. We held, for example, that trademarks are private speech, notwithstanding the government's substantial involvement in the registration process. And, this Court held that flags flown outside of Boston's City Hall did not constitute government speech in part because the city regularly permitted private groups to freely fly their own colors. In all these cases, the controlling question was whether "the government intends to speak for itself or to regulate private expression."

Put in those simple terms, and in light of our precedents, California's attempt to require private individuals in privately accredited CME courses to run implicit-bias training is an evident attempt "to regulate private expression." … First, California has not historically used CME to communicate government messages. While the State requires that CME courses generally relate to the practice of medicine and occasionally requires that courses cover certain subjects, California has not otherwise dictated the content of courses.

Second, because California "relie[s] on the participation of private parties in executing the CME scheme," the public is unlikely to perceive a private instructor's CME course as government speech. As the Ninth Circuit acknowledged, Dr. Khatibi "plausibly alleged facts suggesting that attendees treat her as the person responsible for CME content."

Third, while California extensively regulates the medical field, licenses physicians, and sets the requirements for credit-eligible CME, there is little evidence that California "shape[s] the messages" communicated in CME courses. Despite its long recitation of California regulations, the Ninth Circuit did not identify any state law that requires private speakers in a CME course to express a particular viewpoint—even on contestable medical issues. The implicit-bias-training requirement is a notable departure from that practice. It should have been easy, then, for the courts below to conclude that California's implicit-bias-training requirement regulates private speech.

More troubling than the Ninth Circuit's misapplication of the Shurtleff factors are the implications of the court's decision. On the Ninth Circuit's view of government speech, could California require a CME instructor to communicate the State's preferred message on the availability of abortion? Could the State require a CME instructor to inform participants that for certain patients, gender-transition surgery is ethically required?

What of other professions whose members California licenses and regulates? At the next statewide legal conference at which lectures are offered for continuing legal education, could California require a keynote speaker to oppose racial preferences in law firm hiring? Applying the Ninth Circuit's logic, enough government regulation of the field would convert the private speaker's message in each of these hypotheticals into government speech unprotected by the First Amendment. That result does not follow from this Court's precedents, and it certainly does not follow from the Constitution….

If the Ninth Circuit's decision is truly the kind of result that Shurtleff's three-factor test countenances, we should reconsider Shurtleff. Before Shurtleff, this Court had identified history, public perception, and government control as "relevant" but not mandatory "considerations" for identifying government speech. When Shurtleff described those considerations as a three-factor test, several Members of the Court—myself included—warned that the test would be unworkable and obscure the central inquiry in government-speech cases: whether the government is speaking or regulating private speech. "[L]ike any factorized analysis," the Shurtleff majority's approach does not "provide a principled way of deciding cases." Worse, myopic focus on the history and scope of government control over speech may give courts the false impression that state regulation can convert private speech into government speech.

After only a few years, those concerns are materializing. The Ninth Circuit relied on California's regulation of CME to conclude that requiring private speakers to communicate a government message was not compelled speech but government speech. That is precisely the paradox predicted by the concurrence in Shurtleff: that "government action that regulates private speech would" now "qualify as government speech unregulated by the First Amendment." But, neither compelled speech nor "[c]ensorship" are "made constitutional by aggressive and direct application." It cannot be the case that compelled speech becomes government speech because the government has compelled the speech.

I would grant certiorari to correct course. In my view, the relevant inquiry in a government-speech case is straightforward: Is the government "speaking," or is it "regulating private expression"? The challenged government activity must be "government speech in the literal sense—purposeful communication of a governmentally determined message by a person acting within the scope of a power to speak for the government." Moreover, "the government must … not rely on a means that abridges the speech of persons acting in a private capacity," because doing so reveals that the government has moved from the role of speaker to that of regulator.

Under this framework, it is easy to see why California's law is subject to First Amendment scrutiny. The State's implicit-bias-training requirement is not speech by any government actor; it is a requirement that private speakers communicate certain messages. Although the government may "deputiz[e] private persons as its agents" to convey its message, Dr. Khatibi and Do No Harm's members have not "voluntarily assumed" "a public or quasi-public capacity that empowers them to speak on behalf of the government." They share their own messages through the CME courses they create and deliver, and they do so in their private capacities. Even "government speech in the literal sense is not exempt from First Amendment attack if it uses a means that restricts private expression," such as "compelled speech." When, as here, the government does not issue its own messages but instead requires private speakers to communicate the government's viewpoint, the First Amendment applies….

A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny. We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as "a cover for censorship" or a cloak for compelled speech.

#7626. Why the American West Is the Perfect Setting for a Crime Novel

Before we can answer the question of why the American West is the perfect place for a crime story, we need to clarify what the American West is. This is necessary because there seems to be a great deal of confusion on the subject. You can see this in almost any man-on-the-street interview which quickly reveals that the average American’s understanding of geography is less a body of knowledge than it is a collection of strangely confident opinions. For instance, people who live where I do, in Nevada, might look at Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington and think, “You people are practically sharing a driveway.” Similarly, many people who live along the Eastern Seaboard believe that anything west of the Mississippi River qualifies as the West.

For purposes of crime fiction, I propose that the American West should be considered any place that meets all five of the following criteria:

(1) It’s a Place Where Nobody Can Hear You Scream

I’m not kidding. The West has a lot of empty space. In Tallahassee or Atlanta, if someone screams at 2:17 a.m., seventeen people call 911. In Nevada, there may not be another person within 47 miles. This is both atmospheric and convenient for murder. And for crime authors. The amount of open space is incomprehensible to people who live in tighter confines and where the horizon often consists of a strip mall, a water tower and a billboard advertising personal injury attorneys.

Now, don’t get me wrong. There are a lot of desolate areas out here. But while there might not be any humans within earshot of your scream, rest assured the coyotes, wolves, bears, and other high school mascots can hear you. When you scream in the West, be careful, lest you inadvertently ring the dinner bell for some other kind of serial killer.

(2) It’s a Place Where You Can Hide a Body Almost Anywhere

When human remains are discovered in urban areas, there’s a good chance they’ve haven’t been hidden for more than ten minutes. That’s because there’s no good place to dispose of them without being caught on someone’s cell phone video. If you hope to hide your victim, you have to have a space in grandma’s wall or have a large, airtight cooler. In the West, you have deserts and mountains, some with places where no human has ever left a track. You have canyons so vast that the chances of finding a body begin to depend more on plate tectonics than police work. You have ghost towns with mine shafts so deep that any body placed in one will have to be carbon-dated if and when it’s ever found.

(3) It’s a Place Where Everyone Has a Truck

This solves an enormous number of plot problems for western crime authors. Need to transport a body? Truck. Need to follow someone into the wilderness? Truck. Need your protagonist to spend three chapters driving while contemplating the meaning of life? Truck.

Why does everyone in the American West have a truck, you ask? Because daily life demands one. Just watch any of those YouTube channels featuring people who camp in places a normal vehicle could never get to. I’m convinced many of these YouTube campers are serial killers. Also, in a lot of places, there are so few people that everybody knows everybody, so any crime committed has to be hidden where the eyes of prying neighbors aren’t focused. To get there, you need a truck. Trust me.

(4) It’s a Place Where Everyone Owns a Gun

As a writer of crime fiction, this is particularly useful because you can eliminate several pages of explanation.

In the American West, there are more guns than there are people. Most people own multiple firearms, and children are introduced to them shortly after learning to walk. Sometimes earlier. You may argue the merits of this…until little Tommy uses that .22 you bought him to shoot the rattlesnake that’s about to bite his sister. If, some years later, Tommy turns that same rifle on a person, well, that’s the makings of a pretty good crime story.

(5) It’s Place That Gives Your Detective Something Beautiful to Look at While Brooding

And this is, perhaps, the most important thing. The West is practically a literary service.

Mountain ranges. Sunsets. Deserts. Snow. Big sky. Canyons.

A detective in the West is never more than a few minutes away from something worth staring at while contemplating a murder, a missing person, a regrettable decision or the general decline of civilization.

Try doing that on the Jersey Turnpike. A detective there walks outside, looks dramatically into the distance and sees a Wawa.

The West gives a crime novelist something even more than just scenery: space. Space for a crime to happen. Space for a secret to survive. Space for a suspect to disappear. Space for a sheriff to chase him. And, most importantly, space for a character to stand on a ridge at sunset and wonder what the hell happened to his life.

For me, geography is everything. It’s as much a character in my novels as my protagonist, Porter Beck. When I build an outline for a new story, I plot the scenery just as I do my character biographies. I plot the time of year, the colors, the smells, the flora and fauna. In some cases – most actually – the physical setting is as much an adversary to Beck as the person he’s trying to stop. It might be snow drifts or wildfires or the relentless summer heat.

It’s the opportunities this landscape provides that make the American West the perfect place to stage a crime novel. Out here, there is room for everything a crime story needs.

BRUCE BORGOS lives and writes from the Nevada desert where he works hard every day to prove his high school guidance counselor had good instincts when he said “You’ll never be an astronaut.” He has a degree in political science which mostly served to dissuade him from a career in law while at the same time tormenting his wife with endless questions about how telephones work. When not writing, you can usually find him at the local wine store. He is the author of The Bitter Past.

#7625. Top Dallas County investigator arrested, charged with wife’s murder

Jimmy Harold Spurger Jr., 54, the chief investigator for the Dallas County public defender’s office, was arrested and charged with first-degree murder Saturday after his wife was found dead in their apartment. (Photo from the Dallas County Sheriff’s Department)

The chief investigator for the Dallas County public defender’s office was arrested and charged with first-degree murder Saturday after his wife was found dead in their apartment.

Jimmy Harold Spurger Jr., 54, who has worked for the public defender’s office for nearly 14 years, was married to his wife, Maria Teresa Spurger, for 35 years but filed for divorce in late October, according to Fox 4.

Local first responders who were conducting a welfare check Friday night forced their way into the apartment, where they found Spurger’s wife unresponsive on a couch with a knife in her neck, Fox 4 reports. Spurger also was found in the apartment, covered in blood and sitting next to a knife in the bedroom.

After responding officers found multiple pill bottles also covered in blood, they suspected that Spurger had ingested pills and transported him to the hospital, Fox 4 reports. He was later taken into custody and is being held on a $1 million bond.

Spurger has led the Investigative Division for the Dallas County public defender’s office for 11 months, Fox 4 reports. Previously, he spent more than 13 years in its Capital Murder Division. He also worked for more than 20 years in law enforcement, which included supervising investigations in the Child Abuse and Family Violence Division of the Dallas County district attorney’s office.

Dallas County Chief Public Defender Christi Dean told Fox 4 that Spurger was “an exemplary colleague,” and that “it’s hard to imagine that he has been charged with murder.”

“We know in our profession that the probable cause affidavit doesn’t tell the whole story,” Dean also reportedly said. “The media reports don’t tell the whole story. And we’re still in preliminary stages.”

#7624. Justice Thomas on the Second Amendment in "Sensitive Places"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Justice Thomas's statement respecting the denial of certiorari in Novotny v. Moore:

Maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places. Under Maryland law, an individual may not carry a firearm in public demonstrations, mass transit, places of amusement, healthcare facilities, locations that sell alcohol for onsite consumption, and tens of thousands of acres of state park and forest land. The Fourth Circuit upheld these restrictions against petitioners' Second Amendment challenge because it concluded that each law banned firearms in a "sensitive place."

I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari. Because each Maryland statute implicates a distinct historical tradition of firearm regulation, the breadth of petitioners' challenge would complicate our review. In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however, we should consider the scope of States' authority to ban firearms in "sensitive places."

The Second Amendment recognizes the people's "inherent" right to keep and bear firearms, a right that admits of only historically grounded exceptions. Before and after the founding, it was well understood that individuals enjoyed a natural right to keep and bear arms, which included the right to carry firearms in public spaces for self-defense. The Constitution "codified [that] pre-existing right." The first generations after the founding recognized the breadth of the Second Amendment's "guarante[e]," and "those who sought to carry firearms publicly and peaceably in antebellum America were generally free to do so." Thus, when a State seeks to restrict the right to bear arms—including by limiting the places in which a law-abiding citizen may carry his firearm—the State must root its law in the Second Amendment's "historical understanding" by "demonstrat[ing] that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation."

This Court has previously acknowledged a limited tradition of States' regulating the right to carry firearms in certain "sensitive places." In Bruen, we observed that early American legislatures sometimes prohibited weapons in "legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses." But, we emphasized that this tradition was narrow. "[T]he historical record yields relatively few 18th- and 19th-century 'sensitive places' where weapons were altogether prohibited." While "courts can use analogies to those historical regulations of 'sensitive places' to determine that modern regulations … are constitutionally permissible," "expanding the category of 'sensitive places' … to all places of public congregation … would eviscerate the general right to publicly carry arms for self-defense."

Nevertheless, States have seized on the idea of "sensitive places" to prohibit the peaceable carry of firearms in locations that bear little resemblance to legislatures, polling places, or courthouses. New Jersey, for example, prohibits firearms in at least 25 locations, including zoos, public libraries, casinos, and state-owned beaches. New York has designated 20 locations as "sensitive," ranging from "any place of worship" to "residential settings licensed … by the department of health." California's 29 gun-free spaces include "athletic facilit[ies]," "financial institution[s]," and any government-permitted "public gathering or special event." {Several other States ban firearms in many public places.} These restrictions stand on questionable historical ground. And, their cumulative effect is to prohibit firearms wherever people gather for eating, drinking, recreation, amusement, and free speech—an affront to the right of "law-abiding citizens" to "carr[y] arms in public for" their "ordinary self-defense."

The lower courts have largely blessed these ahistorical ventures. The Fourth Circuit below upheld all but one of Maryland's locational restrictions. A now-vacated decision of the Third Circuit upheld many of New Jersey's "sensitive-place" laws. Courts of Appeals have also rejected challenges to specific locational restrictions in New York, California, and Hawaii.

I harbor serious doubts that our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions. In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry.

#7621. Rhys Bowen on writing real people and settings in historical fiction

One of the aspects of the Royal Spyness series that readers like is that it involves the British royal family in the 1930s. The Prince of Wales, Mrs. Simpson the king and queen, the little princesses walk across the pages and are part of the plots. Other well-known real characters also are featured: Coco Chanel in a couple of books, Noel Coward in several and even Agatha Christie helps solve a mystery in From Cradle to Grave. My fictional heroine is supposedly related to the royals, a great granddaughter of Queen Victoria and thus a cousin first cousin once removed to the Prince of Wales.

Introducing real people to my plots is a bit of a risk, I suppose, but I am by no means unique. Shakespeare certainly wrote about plenty of real people but he retold their true lives. Taking a real person and putting them into a fictional plot is a little different. It is stretching truth and not everybody will be happy with that.

When I started the series I had to think how far I wanted to go from what we know of these characters and I decided I wanted to keep as close as possible to what I knew they said and felt. Queen Mary was a stickler for rules and passionate about antiques so in one plot I had her charge my heroine with reclaiming an antique that had been stolen from her.

I suppose the one person I took the most liberties with was Mrs. Simpson. Since I knew she had a sharp tongue and could be very cruel I enjoyed making her quite unpleasant for several books until she ends up helping my heroine.

Using real people and real settings requires a lot of research. I have to confess that I have poked into every corner of Buckingham Palace, and Kensington Palace, read all the biographies of Chanel and Noel Coward, the Prince of Wales and Mrs Simpson. To me it is important to recreate a real person as faithfully as possible.

In writing about real people each author has to decide how far they want to go and in what ways they might deviate from truth.  Some writers have taken real people and made them sleuths. Stephanie Baron made Jane Austen (very successfully) into a sleuth. Karen Harper had  Queen Elizabeth I solve crimes. Gyles Brandreth makes Oscar Wilde a detective.

Did any of these people really have time to do a little detecting on the side? And without being observed? Jane Austen clearly could have been a good sleuth with her powers of observation of the human condition, especially as she would have been overlooked, sitting in a corner as an unmarried woman. But Queen Elizabeth was accompanied every second of the day.  Could she have found time and opportunity to sleuth a little?

So is the writer allowed to take real people and make them do things they didn’t do? Is there a chance of getting sued? Apparently not if they were a public figure. I could include Agatha Christie in my book, doing what she did best…solve a crime. But I don’t know about making them do something they would never have done: make them a murderer? I think the family would have cause to bring a lawsuit if a respectable person was defamed.

I don’t think I would be comfortable with making a real person do things I know they didn’t do. In fact it gives me great pleasure in having real characters say things I knew they really said. It’s like weaving reality and fiction together.

My favorite example is when Lady Georgie meets her cousins Princess Elizabeth and Princess Margaret. Margaret is three at the time. Georgie says “Hello Margaret,” and Margaret replies, “You have to say Princess Margaret because I’m a princess.” To this Georgie says, “Then you have to say Lady Georgie to me because I’m a lady.”

Margaret looks up at her governess and asks, “Is a lady better than a princess?” To which her governess replies, “One hopes a princess will grow up to be a lady.” True story!

For me the appeal of using real characters and putting my fictional heroine into a real world is that it immediately gives her credibility. It justifies her existence. She’s moving through a real society so we now believe she is real. We know all about Edward VIII and Mrs Simpson and we see Lady Georgie interacting with them. So we accept Lady Georgie as real. Very satisfying.

As well as involving real people in my stories I have introduced real events. We were at Sandringham for the last days of King George V. We were with Mrs Simpson when the king decided to abdicate.

In this latest book in the Royal Spyness series, To Crown It All (book twenty!) the whole story centers around a real event: the coronation of King George and Queen Elizabeth in 1937. This was a well-documented event,  It was even filmed. So I made sure I kept every element completely accurate (except for a minor detail of a plot nobody knew about…which might have happened).

I reasoned that my heroine, Lady Georgie, who is the king’s cousin, would be invited to the Abbey and be involved in the coronation, but I didn’t expect her to get so very involved!

I find it very satisfying to recreate real history, to take readers back to a real time and place, but with the slight addition of my fictional sleuth.

Rhys Bowen is the New York Times bestselling author of more than sixty novels, including Mrs. Endicott’s Splendid Adventure, The Rose Arbor, The Paris Assignment, Where the Sky Begins, The Venice Sketchbook, Above the Bay of Angels, The Victory Garden, The Tuscan Child, and In Farleigh Field, the winner of the Lefty Award for Best Historical Mystery Novel and the Agatha Award for Best Historical Novel. Bowen’s work has won sixteen honors to date, including multiple Agatha, Anthony, and Macavity Awards. Her books have been translated into many languages, and she has fans around the world, including more than seventy thousand Facebook followers. A transplanted Brit, Bowen divides her time between California and Arizona. For more information, visit www.rhysbowen.com.

#7617. 7 mysteries that focus on the motive behind crimes

Means, motive, opportunity: they comprise the classic triad of mystery fiction. Of the three features, I appreciate motive as the real heart of a mystery story.

For two decades before I wrote my debut novel, On the Killer’s Trail, I worked in education and libraries. Prior to that, I was a psychology major and a social worker. I have always been fascinated by what makes people tick. While the success of a work of fiction in any genre may depend on the specifics, for me, its true value lies in the universal truths about human experience that it portrays and reveals. In Louise Penny’s words, “crime was deeply human.”

Here are seven novels that focus on motive in a variety of ways.

No one weaves a mystery from its three strands better than the grande dame of crime fiction, Agatha Christie. In Five Little Pigs, a young woman asks Hercule Poirot to investigate the death of her father for which her mother was convicted sixteen years earlier. The evidence at trial was overwhelming and the accused woman’s defense weak.

Shortly before her own death, the mother professed her innocence to her child in a letter. Due to the passage of time, Poirot must depend on character, rather than evidence, to solve the case. He says, “[Character] is the principal interest of all my cases.” The “five little pigs” are the five people, other than the wife, who had the opportunity to kill Amyas Crane, a talented but eminently unlikeable painter.

Initially, none of the five appears to have a motive to murder him. Poirot tells one of the suspects, “the reason for murder is nearly always to be found by a study of the person murdered.” As Poirot delves into the past, he uncovers the truth about Crane’s life and learns that each of the five did, indeed, have a motive. His analysis of the behavior and motivations of several of the suspects ultimately leads him to the solution.

More than sixty years after Christie’s novel was published, Louise Penny introduces another wise Francophone inspector, Armande Gamache. He, too, investigates the murder of an artist.

The puzzle in Still Life is that, unlike Christie’s victim, Jane Neal of the idyllic Quebecois village of Three Pines was beloved by all. When Neal’s body is found in the woods, felled by an arrow, on Thanksgiving morning, Gamage asks, “who would want to kill kindness?” He later explains “most premeditated murders were about rancid emotions, greed, jealousy, fear, all repressed.”

Penny introduces us to a host of Three Pines villagers, among whom are both suspects and others who will become fond recurring characters in future books, the twenty-first of which was just published this fall.

Sal, a lonely sixth-grade boy, discovers the burned body of middle-school teacher Adam Merkel in the Nevada desert. Merkel had befriended the traumatized boy who came to live on a nearby ranch with his reclusive uncles after the death of his mother.

When one of Adam’s colleagues, who is dealing with her own personal issues, takes it upon herself to investigate, she uncovers secrets in Adam’s past as she also senses that Sal knows more about Adam’s death than he will admit. Her consideration of possible motives explores how the past and present are immutably intertwined.

Sixteen-year-old Lydia Lee has gone missing. When her body is found in a local lake, her devastated parents need to know how and why it happened. Was it a drowning accident, suicide, or foul play?

While this moving novel is not a mystery in the traditional sense, it is an exquisite portrayal of how we are shaped by our families and our experiences and how our motives and actions arise from them. As the family’s emotions and secrets long held in silence are slowly and painfully brought to light, we learn the secrets that Lydia, her siblings, her parents, and their parents have harbored, which ultimately reveal Lydia’s fate.

This historical legal mystery is set in a small town in 1946 Mississippi. Pete Banning is an upright, church-going model citizen and World War II hero. After returning from the Philippines and the horrors of his war experience there, he hopes to resume the life he left behind with his wife Liza and their children on their cotton farm. When he has Liza committed to a psychiatric hospital and, soon after, calmly shoots his pastor and friend, Dexter Belland, Banning refuses to defend himself, stating only, “I have nothing to say.”

Inspired by an actual case from the 1930’s in which the defendant made the same statement until his execution, Grisham keeps the reader guessing until the end why Banning is prepared to die, rather than reveal his motive.

A murder mystery within a murder mystery. Editor Susan Ryeland receives the manuscript of her client, author Alan Conway’s latest mystery novel featuring detective Atticus Pund, but with the story’s ending missing.

When Conway is found dead, Ryeland concludes that the manuscript involves real-life events and that Conway’s murderer stole the final pages to avoid incrimination. Ryeland sets out to find the motive and perpetrator of Pund’s fictional mystery to find Conway’s real-life killer.

Stuart Turton, The 7 ½ Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle

Straddling genres, this mystery borrows from speculative fiction to shift time and perspective as the protagonist investigates a murder from the viewpoints of multiple characters within the setting of a classic English country estate. Aiden Bishop wakes up at Blackheath Manor with amnesia and no knowledge of why he is there.

In each of eight days in a time loop, he finds himself inhabiting a different guest at the manor until he can solve the murder of the young heiress of the estate, Evelyn Hardcastle, who died that evening. If he cannot solve the case by the end of day eight, he is doomed to repeat the cycle with his memory wiped clean.

Whatever the setting or sub-genre, the key to a murder mystery is motive. As Inspector Armande Gamage put it, “My job is to find people who take lives. And to do that, I have to find out why.”

Alice Openshaw has been a fan of mysteries since the age of ten, when she discovered Perry Mason books at her tiny town’s public library. She holds a BA in psychology from Middlebury College in Vermont and an MLS from Vanderbilt University. She lived in rural Maine for thirty years, where she worked as a librarian and adult literacy teacher and raised three children and an assortment of animals on a small farm. She now lives near Cape Cod, Massachusetts, with her husband and her tuxedo cat, Frankie. On the Killer's Trail is her debut novel.

#7616. Catherine Townsend on treating dating like detective work, and vice versa

When I was a dating columnist for The Independent in London, I would often point out the similarities between dating and detective work. I’d flag that in both scenarios, you find yourself sitting in front of a stranger—the difference being that in a potential love match, the skeletons in their closet are (hopefully) merely metaphorical, rather than decomposing in a crawl space.

The same logic works in reverse. Conducting investigative interviews is, in crucial ways, very much like being on one long and strange first date. The idea is to ask open-ended questions and to encourage the person you are trying to get information from to keep talking about themselves. If they keep talking, eventually you can find the inconsistencies in their story.

A more cynical take would be that falling in love is like one long con. When we like someone, our brain is wired to look for commonalities. And the more we like someone, the more we mimic their behavior. This works extremely well for getting someone to trust you— and that is why con artists mimic our movements, too, for less pure reasons.

But my job when I’m conducting an interview is to see the worst in people.

In 2010, I was living in Los Angeles, had just enrolled in PI school with Dale, and was moonlighting as a PI. State boards give credit to-ward investigative hours for police work, which is why retired police detectives can qualify as licensed private investigators. But, despite the fact that investigative journalism uses a lot of the same skill sets as detective work, journalists are given zero credit for hours worked in newsrooms.

My first encounters with law enforcement had been less than satisfactory, and I was convinced that this was because, for the most part, they didn’t trust the media. So I wanted to get some more specialized training, something that would raise my skill levels and, hopefully, my esteem in the eyes of the police departments that I was trying to sweet-talk.

Living in Los Angeles, the quintessential sunny place for shady people, is like having permanent residence inside a noir mystery painted with the rainbow neon sunsets, and traffic jams, of Grand Theft Auto V.

Dale sent me out on a lot of matrimonial surveillances, and they almost always unfolded in the same way.

Sometimes, the clients would summon me to their homes. But, following the detective manual logic on interrogations, I preferred to coax the clients into nonthreatening, neutral territory—preferably one that invoked feelings of nostalgia. I found that magic location sliding into a red leatherette booth at Bob’s Big Boy diner in Burbank at sunrise, sipping a ten-ounce mug of Big Boy medium roast, and watching the pink clouds float across an impossibly bright, Monet-meets-vaporwave California sky.

After that, things usually get complicated. The client asks me to follow their boyfriend/husband/girlfriend/married boyfriend who also has another girlfriend but has promised that they are his only mistress. (I pretend to ignore the logical fallacies of that argument.) I ask them what they hope to accomplish from a surveillance.

I’m honest: I’ll tell them that it’s expensive, uncertain, and a hell of a lot harder than it looks on TV. (If you don’t believe me, try identifying a subject described as “white man in a suit” outside a downtown office building at night from a fuzzy Facebook photo. Bonus points if it’s a rainy winter night and only a few inches of skin are visible!)

I’ll also ask them why they believe that their loved one has been unfaithful, and often they will tell me something that lets me know that they already know the truth: Maybe they have found a topless selfie of his secretary, or a scrap of lacy women’s underwear in the glove compartment of his Prius.

I try to always have these conversations over something sweet, which is why I prefer to meet at restaurants. I load the table with strawberry waffles or a banana milkshake with extra maraschino cherries, since bad news goes down easier with a heavy dose of sugar lubricant. Even Cinnabon at the mall food court is better than nothing: Studies show that our animal brains associate the smells of cinnamon and vanilla with comfort and security.

“Well, it sounds like you already know the answer,” I inevitably say. Why would you think that this is a good person, despite mounting evidence to the contrary?

Before I dig in and disrupt lives, potentially unearthing a truth that could shake the foundations of a person’s existence, I always ask the same question: Do you really want to know? Little white lies can be the glue that holds relationships together. No, you don’t look fat in those white jeans. Yes, you’re the best sex I’ve ever had.

I make a point of sliding one of my Patrick Bateman-style thick business cards across the table and making a reference to The Matrix: Would they rather take the blue pill and remain blissfully ignorant, or the red pill to see where the rabbit hole, however unpleasant, leads?

Some people have a compulsive need to know the reality, however brutal and disruptive it will be to their existence, and they will continue to pick it apart like an overeager esthetician digging out blackheads on YouTube. And then there are those who decide that for whatever reason—long marriage, double mortgage, social hierarchy, or something else—they want to stay inside the much happier bubble they have created.

Before you ask a question that could shatter your reality forever, it’s important to know which camp you fall into. Because once the bubble is pierced, it’s almost impossible to get back in—and if a person chooses to overlook a betrayal, an infidelity, or something worse, lying to themselves afterward can become a full-time job.

Catherine Townsend is a journalist, private investigator, and podcaster. She is the host of the iHeartMedia podcast Hell and Gone and Red Collar. After beginning her career as a staff writer for New York Magazine, Catherine moved to London to create The Independent’s very popular “Sleeping Around” dating column. Her articles have appeared in publications including The Atlantic, Elle, New York, GQ, Marie Claire, Cosmopolitan, The Daily Mail, The New York Post, Investigation Discovery, and HuffPost. She became a licensed private investigator in 2013. She is the author of How to Survive a Murder Investigation: A True Story of Death and Danger in the Ozarks.

#7613. Op-Ed: Crime Drops—Locally Collected Data Drives National Headlines

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

This opinion piece by CJIS Special Agent in Charge Timothy A. Ferguson was published by the Bridgeport News on October 19, 2026.

Across the country, you saw the headlines. Violent crime declined historically last year—dropping an estimated 9.3% from 2024 to 2025. Murder and nonnegligent manslaughter estimated offenses saw an even larger dip of 18.1%.

In West Virginia, crime was also trending downward.

These headlines are based on data reported to the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program by more than 17,000 agencies, covering 96.2% of the U.S. population. It is the responsibility of the FBI’s UCR Program, located within the Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division, in Clarksburg, West Virginia, to collect and publish the data from all 50 states to provide a national picture of reported crime.

This is no small feat. Every day, states and agencies translate local and state crime categories into the national standard and submit their data to the FBI. The UCR Program publishes this data monthly on the Crime Data Explorer to promote transparency and allow you to view timely crime data.

The program also uses the data to develop special reports on topics that matter to you — such as crime in schools, aggravated assault with a firearm, and teen/domestic violence. Then once a year, the program sorts through more than 700 million data points to present you the annual snapshot of crime.

Data collection is just a small fraction of what is accomplished at the CJIS Division. Other efforts also make headlines or prevent you from seeing a tragedy on the news.

Tips actioned by the National Threat Operations Center (NTOC) stop school shootings and help with investigations. Super intelligence capabilities incorporated into NTOC enhance the speed and precision of tip triage, strengthening our ability to process the highest priority tips first so we can promptly share critical threat information with federal, state, and local law enforcement.

Criminal history information from the Interstate Identification Index prevents criminals from becoming your child’s teacher or bus driver. Wants and warrants within the National Crime Information Center help police arrest violent criminals.

Detectives can identify subjects and victims through fingerprints submitted to the Next Generation Identification System.

The division’s mission is to provide our partners with the criminal justice information they need while preserving civil liberties. Sharing that information with officers on the frontlines results in arrests that take criminals off the street and keep neighborhoods safe.

It helps law enforcement return to their families at the end of their shifts. It crushes violent crime and defends the homeland.

When you see headlines of declining crime, know the work to determine that, and the investigations that preceded it, are touched by your neighbors dedicated to the mission at the FBI’s CJIS Division.

Timothy A. Ferguson is assistant director in charge of the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division in Clarksburg, West Virginia. CJIS provides vital systems and services to local, state, tribal, and federal agencies that help ensure public safety. These include the National Crime Information Center; the FBI’s Next Generation Identification System and associated biometric services; the National Instant Criminal Background Check System for firearm purchases; the National Threat Operations Center, which receives and processes tips from the public; and the Uniform Crime Reporting Program, which publishes crime and law enforcement statistical data.

Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is currently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS.

“Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in New York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”

“We will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious ISIS ideology wherever they may be found,” said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”

“Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”

Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.

The first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.

An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the New York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.

This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia Field Office.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.

#7609. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”

#7607. Lindsay Clancy loses bid to dismiss murder case with retrial possibility

Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children and claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Photo by CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via the Associated Press)

Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, lost her bid to have her case dismissed Monday, setting the stage for a possible retrial.

Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan’s 17-page ruling found that a retrial would not be considered double jeopardy because Clancy’s initial jury was deadlocked.

Clancy, 36, was on trial earlier this year for the strangling deaths of her three young children. The case ended in a mistrial after one juror, known as “Juror Doe,” held out for a conviction. Clancy pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, alleging that she was going through postpartum psychosis at the time of the tragedy, according to coverage on Courthouse News Service.

Last week, a hearing seeking dismissal of the case explored the role of Michael Desronvil, who is referred to as “Juror Doe” in court records. Desronvil was accused of not following the court’s instructions.

Sullivan found that the evidence “did not reasonably suggest Juror Doe’s inability to deliberate or refusal to follow the law.”

On Nov. 2, the prosecution said it intends to try Clancy again. She initially faced three counts of murder for the deaths of Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months.

#7606. Justice Department Announces Results from Operation Not Forgotten 2026

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice and FBI announced today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered.  FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations.  Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

“The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”

“This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

“Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” said Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”

“Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” said Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come."

Examples of cases charged during this period include:

In the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses.  Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.  In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.

In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.

In the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.

In the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo.  His case is pending trial.

Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.

In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.

Operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.

This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.

During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.

Additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a new FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI announced the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.

The FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.

The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at https://tips.fbi.gov.

#7602. What happened at Weil Gotshal? Could tech help other firms avoid that fate?

November 11, 2026, 9:17 am CST By Victor Li

There have been plenty of law firm failures over the years. For instance, there was a run on closures thanks to the Great Recession, and Dewey & LeBoeuf’s 2012 failure sent shockwaves throughout the industry.

But when Weil, Gotshal & Manges announced last month that it would be winding down operations, it felt different compared to the others before.

After all, many of the BigLaw firms that went out of the business during the Great Recession had been overexposed in certain areas, and when the housing market crashed, so did their business. Dewey’s failure happened for a lot of reasons, mainly due to big money guarantees to partners, an ill-advised merger, and alleged financial irregularities that resulted in criminal indictments.

Weil Gotshal, though, had long been a firm with one of the best reputations on Wall Street, let alone the world. How did a firm like that end up joining the others on the dustheap? And could technology play a role in helping other firms avoid such a fate in the future?

In this episode of the Legal Rebels Podcast, Noah Waisberg talks to the ABA Journal’s Victor Li about those and other topics. Waisberg is the co-founder and the CEO of Zuva—an artificial intelligence contract analysis platform—and a longtime advocate of using technology to review contracts. He’s also a former Weil Gotshal associate, having worked there as a summer associate in 2005 and then as an associate from 2006 to 2010.

Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure

Weil Gotshal to wind down in shock fall for heavyweight firm

Noah Waisberg is the co-founder and the CEO of Zuva—an artificial intelligence contract analysis platform—and a longtime advocate of using technology to review contracts. He’s also a former Weil, Gotshal & Manges associate, having worked there as a summer associate in 2005 and then as an associate from 2006 to 2010. Before leading Zuva, Waisberg was the CEO of Kira Systems, the leading contract analysis company for professional service agencies, from its founding to its sale to Litera in 2021.

#7601. Maryland Man Convicted of $18.7 Million Medicare Fraud for Respiratory Testing Scheme Targeting Nursing Homes

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

“Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” said U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”

“This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

Through his company, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

The jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.
